method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1' (published 13 January 2023), 25 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9845795). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038) 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas' (published 27 April 2024), 12 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License) (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11398946). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every ERN GENTURIS 2023 claim (S1, quoted) unchanged and adds S2, a 2024 European modified-Delphi consensus (10 experts) on preventing and managing selumetinib adverse events in children with NF1 plexiform neurofibromas, paraphrased because it is CC BY-NC. Its consensus table (Table 1) and dose-modification table (Supplementary Table 2) were not machine-read. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Table 1 (the surveillance summary). S1 Tables 2–15 and S2 Table 1 have merged cells and were not extracted.

claims.claim: **NF1 is autosomal dominant, with a birth incidence of about one in 2000–2500.** About half of patients inherit it; the other half carry a de novo NF1 variant.
claims.source_text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder with an estimated birth incidence of one in 2000-2500. Approximately half of the patients with NF1 have inherited the disorder from their parents, while the other half acquired a de novo pathogenic variant in the NF1 gene.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnosis needs two of the revised criteria:** six or more café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, Lisch nodules or choroidal abnormalities, a characteristic bone dysplasia, a heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant, or a parent with NF1.
claims.source_text: NF1 can be diagnosed using the revised diagnostic criteria which include the presence of two of the following: ≥ six café-au-lait-macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma (OPG), Lisch nodules or choroid abnormalities, bone dysplasia, the presence of a heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant, and the presence of a parent with NF1.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lifetime cancer risk is about 59.6%, against 30.8% in the general population,** and life expectancy is shortened by 8–15 years, mostly through malignancy.
claims.source_text: The lifetime risk of cancer in patients with NF1 was estimated to be 59.6%, compared to 30.8% in the general population. … The life expectancy of patients with NF1 is generally decreased by 8-15 years, mainly due to malignancies.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Management decisions belong with a multidisciplinary team that includes an NF1 expert.**
claims.source_text: decisions about management should be discussed in multidisciplinary teams including an NF1 expert.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Children up to ten years: clinical assessment every year. Over ten: at least every two years.**
claims.source_text: For children up to ten years annual assessments to detect complications of NF1 are advised. Children older than ten years require clinical assessments at least once every two years
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eyes:** until age eight, children without a known optic pathway glioma should be examined by an ophthalmologist experienced in NF1; after eight, formal visual screening every year until adulthood.
claims.source_text: In addition, children until the age of eight years without a known OPG, should be examined by trained paediatric ophthalmologists, neuro-ophthalmologists, or someone with equivalent experience in the assessment of NF1 related visual changes. In children older than eight years without known OPG formal annual visual screening is advised until adulthood.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eye checks up to age 8 (S1 summary table):** visual assessment, fundoscopy and visual fields at least yearly (strong, strong and moderate), and optical coherence tomography when feasible (moderate); from 8 until the move to adult care, yearly visual screening (moderate). An orbital or periorbital plexiform neurofibroma needs refraction, visual fields and eye movements checked at every visit, at any age (strong).

claims.claim: **At every visit, at any age (S1 summary table):** look for signs of a brain or spinal tumour (moderate), cutaneous neurofibromas (strong), plexiform neurofibromas (moderate), MPNST or atypical neurofibroma (strong), glomus tumours of the fingers and toes by asking about symptoms and inspecting (moderate), and psychosocial and neuropsychological needs (weak). Under 12, watch for juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia through the usual history and examination (moderate). From adolescence, examine for GIST, and image the abdomen with MRI or CT only if symptoms suggest one (moderate).

claims.claim: **Adults: clinical assessment at least every three years,** covering history, signs of brain tumour or MPNST, skin neurofibromas and plexiform neurofibromas.
claims.source_text: This guideline recommends that adults with NF1 should be assessed clinically, at least once every three years (Table 1, Table 2). Every visit should consist of history taking, examination for signs/symptoms of brain tumours or MPNSTs, examination of the skin for cutaneous neurofibromas, and screening for/monitoring of plexiform neurofibromas.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Whole-body MRI at least once at the transition to adulthood** to measure internal plexiform tumour burden (a predictor of MPNST). If it shows no internal plexiform neurofibromas, repeat WB-MRI is not needed.
claims.source_text: Monitoring for plexiform neurofibromas should exist of WB-MRI imaging at least once at transition from childhood to adulthood to evaluate internal tumour burden as a predictor for MPNSTs. In the absence of internal plexiform neurofibromas on WB-MRI, further monitoring using WB-MRI is not recommended.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **MRI is the preferred imaging; avoid CT in children where possible** to limit radiation in a population already at raised cancer risk.
claims.source_text: Since the population with NF1 already has an increased risk of developing cancer, limiting diagnostic radiation exposure in this population is recommended. Therefore, the use of CT should be avoided in children with NF1 when possible and when used should be carefully considered.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Plexiform neurofibromas occur in about 40–60% of people with NF1.**
claims.source_text: Plexiform neurofibromas are benign, diffuse or nodular growing tumours of the nerve sheath arising in approximately 40-60% of patients with NF1
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Surgery should be considered for a symptomatic plexiform neurofibroma, with closer monitoring; if it is symptomatic and inoperable, a MEK inhibitor may be considered.**
claims.source_text: Surgery should be considered for symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas, and increased monitoring is recommended., For symptomatic, inoperable symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas in patients with NF1 MEK inhibitors may be considered.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **New pain, a change in texture or a sudden increase in growth of a plexiform neurofibroma means evaluate for malignant change.**
claims.source_text: In case of pain, change in texture or sudden increase in growth, the plexiform neurofibroma should be evaluated for possible malignant transformation.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Selumetinib, an oral MEK1/2 inhibitor, is licensed as monotherapy for children with NF1 and symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas:** by the FDA from age 2 (April 2020) and by the EMA from age 3 (June 2021).
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **In the SPRINT phase II trial the commonest adverse effects were nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, asymptomatic CPK rise, acneiform rash and paronychia,** mostly mild; 14 of 50 children (28%) needed a dose reduction and 5 (10%) stopped for toxicity.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Before starting, get a baseline eye examination with fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography (OCT); then repeat every 3–6 months,** more often in younger children. Monthly review may be needed under 6 years, with limited speech, abnormal baseline fundi or reduced acuity, or a progressing optic glioma.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Echocardiography about every 3 months, more often early in treatment,** and at intervals shorter than 3 months if there are other cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, congenital heart disease, high cholesterol, diabetes).
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Creatine phosphokinase (CPK): check it every 1–3 months at first and every 4–6 months later,** making sure the sample is a resting value unaffected by exercise or muscle injury.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Heart:** a fall in LVEF that stays above the age-specific lower limit of normal, without symptoms, needs only continued echo. **Stop selumetinib and refer to cardiology for symptomatic or grade 3–4 LVEF reduction;** if LVEF returns to normal within 3 months it may be restarted at the first reduced dose.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Eyes:** if retinal pigment epithelial detachment or central serous retinopathy is found, consider pausing selumetinib until it resolves, even with normal acuity, and re-examine every 3–4 weeks.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **CPK:** an asymptomatic rise below 5 times the upper limit of normal (grade 1–2) is not a reason to stop. Rhabdomyolysis means stopping permanently, weighed against how fast the tumour is progressing.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Paronychia:** prevent it by protecting hands and feet (no tight shoes, nails not cut short). Treat every grade with antiseptic soaks twice a day (5–20 minutes); for grade 2 add a potent topical steroid once infection is excluded by swab, or a systemic antibiotic if infected; for grade 3 with several nails involved seek podiatry or surgical advice and consider reducing or stopping the drug. The panel waits at least 2 weeks, and until healed, before restarting.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Skin rashes:** for eczematous rash, emollient twice a day and a low-potency topical steroid for 1–2 weeks, stepping up to a stronger steroid after 3–7 days if needed, then a dose reduction. For mild acneiform rash, a topical antibiotic with or without a mild steroid; for severe rash, an oral semisynthetic tetracycline for 2–6 weeks, but topical antibiotics under 8 years; minocycline is not advised. Sun protection helps prevent rash.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Interactions:** avoid fluconazole and itraconazole as systemic antifungals, and avoid omeprazole for gastritis (use another proton pump inhibitor), because each can raise selumetinib levels. For nausea not settled by diet, an antiemetic such as ondansetron can be tried for 2–3 weeks.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Mouth:** prevent stomatitis with twice-daily tooth and tongue brushing, a soft brush replaced at least every 3 months, and no alcohol-based mouthwash; treat early stomatitis with an analgesic or topical nystatin and use mucositis gels for pain.
claims.locator: Azizi AA, Hargrave D, Passos J, Wolkenstein P, et al. (European expert panel, modified Delphi), Neuro-Oncology Practice 2024;11(5):515 (doi 10.1093/nop/npae038), 'Consensus recommendations on management of selumetinib-associated adverse events in pediatric patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and plexiform neurofibromas', published 27 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11398946/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **MPNST lifetime risk is 8–16%, usually diagnosed at age 20–40.**
claims.source_text: Patients with NF1 have an 8-16% lifetime risk of developing MPNSTs at any age; however, it is usually diagnosed between the age of 20-40 years.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Red flags for MPNST:** rapid growth, new persistent substantial pain, new weakness, sensory deficit, sphincter disturbance, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or any change in tumour consistency.
claims.source_text: Clinical assessment should include screening for the following clinical features suggestive for a MPNST: rapid tumour growth, new and persistent, substantial pain, new motor deficit/weakness, sensory deficit, sphincter disturbance, swallowing or breathing difficulty, or any changes in tumour consistency
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If malignancy is suspected, image with 18FDG PET-MRI (or PET-CT if unavailable) plus regional MRI.**
claims.source_text: When malignancy is suspected based on clinical or imaging (MRI) signs, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography magnetic resonance imaging (18FDG PET MRI) (preferred) or 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography computed tomography (18FDG PET CT) (if 18FDG PET MRI is not available) combined with regional MRI is advised.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspected ANNUBP or MPNST: resect primarily when safe;** otherwise take an image-guided biopsy, decided by a sarcoma MDT, because a biopsy can miss the malignant part.
claims.source_text: In case of a suspected ANNUBP or MPNST, primary resection is recommended if safe and feasible. Otherwise, radiologically (preferably 18FDG PET MRI) guided diagnostic biopsy should be performed. This biopsy should be taken at the discretion of a (sarcoma) multidisciplinary team, as tumours can be heterogeneous, with the potential for a false negative result by missing malignant parts of the tumour
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **MPNST treatment is complete excision with wide margins;** chemotherapy and radiotherapy only in specific situations.
claims.source_text: The mainstay of treatment for MPNSTs is complete excision with wide margins; however, chemotherapy and radiotherapy might be considered in specific situations
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Optic pathway gliomas affect up to 15% of children with NF1;** refer every one, symptomatic or not, to an expert unit.
claims.source_text: The incidence of OPGs is as high as 15% in children with NF1 … Any patient with NF1 diagnosed with an asymptomatic or symptomatic OPG should receive a referral to an expert unit for the management of this NF1 associated OPG (e.g. paediatric, ophthalmology, and/or neuro-oncology)
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Low-grade glioma:** complete resection when feasible for symptomatic or progressive tumours; watch and wait if asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic; for inoperable tumours needing treatment use chemotherapy and avoid radiotherapy.
claims.source_text: When feasible, complete resection of the lesion is the best therapeutic option for a symptomatic or progressive LGG (Table 4, Table 5). Asymptomatic LGGs and those with mild symptoms can be followed over time with imaging, a watch-and-wait approach is recommended., For inoperable symptomatic gliomas needing treatment, chemotherapy is recommended, and radiotherapy should be avoided.
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Breast cancer: annual screening from age 30, preferably by breast MRI;** from 50, follow national population screening.
claims.source_text: Annual screening for breast cancer in females with NF1 is advised to start at the age of 30 years preferably by breast MRI (Table 1, Table 11). From the age of 50 years females with NF1 should be screened for breast cancer according to the national guidelines for population screening in their country
claims.locator: European Reference Network for Genetic Tumour Risk Syndromes (ERN GENTURIS), eClinicalMedicine 2023;56:101818, 'ERN GENTURIS tumour surveillance guidelines for individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1', published 13 January 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845795/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma: test biochemically for symptoms, in pregnancy and before elective surgery under general anaesthetic;** routine screening is not recommended.
claims.source_text: Biochemical testing for secreting phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma is recommended when suggestive symptoms are present or during pregnancy and before elective surgery requiring general anaesthesia. … However, routine biochemical screening for phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma in adults with NF1 is not recommended at this moment

claims.claim: **GIST: resect an incidental asymptomatic GIST of 2 cm or more;** smaller ones can be watched with MRI. NF1 GISTs usually lack KIT/PDGFRA changes and do not respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
claims.source_text: If incidentally detected by MRI, resection of asymptomatic GISTs with a diameter of 2 cm or more is recommended. Smaller asymptomatic lesions may be monitored by abdominal MRI (Table 14). NF1-related GISTs typically lack alterations in KIT or PDGFRA, seen in sporadic GISTs, resulting in unresponsiveness to therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

claims.claim: **Screen regularly for psychosocial wellbeing and neuropsychological function,** with a psychologist in the multidisciplinary team.
claims.source_text: Additional to NF1 related tumour treatment and management, regular screening for psychosocial wellbeing and neuropsychological functioning is strongly advised (Table 1, Table 15). To ensure this, it is strongly advised to have a psychologist as a member of the multidisciplinary team, to support patients and families when making decisions about diagnosis, management and treatment
